questions.q: What belongs in the Results section, per this lesson, as opposed to adjectives like 'worked really well'?
options: A list of every job ID submitted during the project
The original hypothesis, restated without any data
Actual numbers and the claim-by-claim analysis -- e.g., 'the reduction was 0.155'
Only a qualitative summary with no numbers
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly contrasts 'the reduction was 0.155' (belongs in Results) with 'mitigation worked really well' (does not) -- Results should report numbers, not adjectives.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a thin or missing limitations section is a red flag, not just a stylistic choice?
options: Because limitations sections are legally required in all research
It was already identified back in Lesson 2 as a sign of an overstated result when reading other people's papers critically
Because readers never actually read limitations sections
Because a thin limitations section always means the data was fabricated
questions.explain: The lesson ties this directly back to Lesson 2's paper-reading red flags: a thin or absent limitations section on a strong claim was identified there as a sign of possible overstatement.

questions.q: In the worked Limitations excerpt, what specific confound was disclosed, and why was it included rather than omitted?
options: A roughly six-hour calibration gap between the original 3- and 5-qubit runs, included because the discrepancy between confounded and corrected results is itself informative
Nothing was disclosed in the Limitations section of the worked excerpt
A completely different hypothesis that was abandoned, included for no stated reason
A missing shot count, included to apologize for sloppy work
questions.explain: The worked excerpt explicitly discloses the six-hour calibration gap and explains that reporting both the confounded and corrected comparisons is itself informative about measurement sensitivity to calibration drift.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a common write-up mistake to avoid?
options: Writing a limitations section with the same care as the results section
Reporting both a confounded and a corrected result with an explanation
Letting the conclusion claim more than the data supports, e.g., generalizing from one device and calibration window to a universal scaling statement
Including a methods section with specific device names and parameters
questions.explain: The lesson lists overgeneralizing the conclusion beyond the data's actual scope as a common mistake -- the other three options are the GOOD practices the lesson recommends, not mistakes.

questions.q: How does the lesson suggest Lesson 19's experiment summary should be used when writing the formal report?
options: Submitted as-is in place of the full formal report
Used only for the title page, with no other content reused
Expanded and organized into the four sections -- methods, results, limitations, conclusions -- rather than generating new content from scratch
Discarded entirely, since the report must start from a blank page
questions.explain: The lesson explains that writing the formal report is mostly a matter of expanding and organizing the experiment summary into the four sections, not generating new content from nothing.
